prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms brought atomic frequency standards to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks as a single-part prize and I have not changed my preferred configuration since round 1. The round-1 exchange sharpened rather than weakened the case. Six members now name the same two laureates, but what persuades me is the science: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is a specific, identifiable invention that removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping many atoms, and Ye's strontium systems turned it into the 10^-18 performance that independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE) now reproduce. That is a discovery or invention with a named origin, which is how I understand the criterion, and not lifetime achievement. The chair asks whether the citation can separate this from the 2005 comb prize. It can: the comb is the readout, whereas the lattice clock is the solution to interrogating many neutral atoms without motional shifts, so I would word the citation around the lattice and the 10^-18 uncertainty and not around precision spectroscopy in general. I also would not wait for the redefinition of the second. That is a metrological decision that follows from the demonstrated performance, and the prize should rest on what has been measured.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains that precision timekeeping has already been recognised in 1989, 2005 and 2012, so a critic can call this a third prize in one neighbourhood. I do not regard that as a bar, since the lattice clock is a distinct invention, but I accept that the citation has to carry the argument. Two names cannot cover Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley, the Yb and Sr groups at RIKEN, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, or ion-clock contributors, and I would want the committee to say openly that the three-person limit forces this choice. Finally, a pure metrology prize has a prospective payoff in the redefinition of the second, which a sceptic will count against it.

responses.point: Pearce proposes a two-part prize, clocks plus IceCube with Halzen alone, but says clocks alone would be cleaner and that he would drop B027 if the single-name attribution does not convince colleagues.
responses.response: I read your fallback as the right instinct, and I would go further. Five of us, including me, have said the one-name credit for a cubic-kilometre collaboration is exposed, and you concede it yourself. I also do not think the diffuse flux and the source identifications can be separated here: the TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068 associations are still at moderate significance, and without them the case is a flux measurement credited to one leader. A second part that dilutes a configuration with six supporters, for a case that its own proposer calls a few years short, weakens the whole prize. I would keep neutrino astronomy for a later year with a fuller credit, and I do not include B027 even as an alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers twisted bilayer graphene because it opened a new class of correlated matter, separates the existence of the discovery from the unsettled pairing mechanism, and argues the clocks only refine a measurement capability already recognised by earlier prizes.
responses.response: Your separation of discovery from mechanism is fair, and I withdraw part of my earlier objection: the open mechanism is not itself a reason to deny recognition, as with high-temperature superconductivity. My remaining difficulty is attribution and timing. Cao as first author and Dean, Young, Yacoby and Efetov are outside the three names, and you grant that the group-leader convention is defensible but open to criticism. I do not accept that the clocks only refine an existing capability. Interrogating many neutral atoms in a lattice at 10^-18 is a new regime, not a smoother version of the comb. I keep B017 as my first alternative and would move it up if the committee thinks the field is stable enough, but I would not give it priority over a configuration that you also call cleaner on attribution.

responses.point: Kroll treats the overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize as a presentational point, keeps B042 and B017 as alternatives, and notes the unresolved Hall-laboratory connection behind his own recusal flag.
responses.response: I agree that the overlap is mainly presentational and that the citation should name the lattice clock explicitly. Where I would go beyond you is on your disclosed doctoral stay in Hall's laboratory: it is a lineage tie to the comb tradition and not to Katori or Ye, and I think the committee can note it without recusing you, since no documented relationship exists with either credited name. On alternatives, you list B042, which I do not, because the split among Bloch, Greiner, Esslinger, Cirac and Zoller between theory and experiment is unresolved and a three-person cut would be arbitrary. I find B017 a more natural second choice than B042 for that reason.

responses.point: Mehlig asks how the citation should balance Katori's concept against Ye's record-accuracy realisation, and notes that Ye's relation to the comb prize must be handled carefully.
responses.response: I would handle it by crediting the pair for the invention and development of the lattice clock, with the citation naming magic-wavelength trapping first and the 10^-18 uncertainty second, so that Katori's concept and Ye's realisation both appear. This also keeps Ye's comb heritage out of the credited achievement, since the citation names the lattice clock and not the readout. I agree with your point on B010: the Kane, Mele, Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Molenkamp and Hasan allocation is too unstable for this year, and I have kept it only as a distant second alternative on that account. I would also resist moving B002 up on the strength of detector leadership, as you do.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts that the lattice clock is a distinct invention from the 2005 and 2012 precedents, or regards a third precision-measurement prize as a repeat; I think the former but cannot rule out the latter.
How the citation should weigh Katori's concept against Ye's record-accuracy systems, and whether omitting Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and others will be read as unfair.
Whether B017 will look clearly stronger once the pairing mechanism and the experimental credit (Cao and others) are better settled, which could be a year or two away.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B001, B017 or B010: my work is transmission electron microscopy of interfaces and oxides, not clocks, moire materials or topological insulators. My only listed Chalmers connection is to Goran Johansson, who no longer prefers B003, and I have no documented tie to Katori, Ye or any other credited name. My oxide-interface work (LaAlO3/SrTiO3) is adjacent to B017 but involves no credited person. I note Kroll's disclosure on B001 and see no reason for recusal.
